Chapter 9: The Importance of Rituals and Saying Goodbye.
You know, rituals—no matter how big or small—have always helped us make sense of loss. The mortician saw this every single day. Families would come together to light candles, share memories, or maybe play a favorite song.
Even the simplest acts gave shape to their grief and helped them find a path forward.
One afternoon, a family showed up carrying a box filled with handwritten letters. Each person had written a note to their grandmother, who always encouraged them to speak from the heart. At the graveside, they took turns reading those letters out loud—there were tears, but also laughter, drifting through the spring air. The mortician watched from a distance, gently reminded that saying goodbye is really about the living, just as much as it is about honoring the person who’s gone.
But not every ritual has to be traditional. Some families chose to scatter ashes in a favorite park, or maybe plant a tree in memory of someone they loved. The mortician remembered a group of friends who gathered at the beach, tossing flowers into the waves as the sun slipped below the horizon. There wasn’t a priest, or any formal ceremony—just a shared moment of remembrance.
What most people don’t realize is just how much freedom they actually have when creating these rituals. The mortician often encouraged families to do what felt right, not just what was expected. And she saw that when people took ownership of the process, their grief somehow became a little easier to carry.
Of course, sometimes, rituals didn’t go as planned—a sudden downpour, a forgotten eulogy, or even a child bursting into laughter at just the wrong moment. The mortician learned to embrace those imperfections. After all, they’re a reminder that life—even right at the end—remains unpredictable and completely real.
